text:
Middle East conflict and Chinese safeguards fuel uptick in Aussie and Kiwi beef made possible by post-Brexit trade deals.

AI generated Text-to-speech

LONDON — British farmers have long warned that free trade deals with Australia and New Zealand would open the floodgates to a wave of cheap, imported meat.

Nearly five years after those deals were signed, farmers say their fears are fast becoming reality.

While Ireland remains Britain’s largest overseas supplier of beef, Australia and New Zealand are steadily gaining market share as tariff-free access expands under the trade deals inked in 2021 and 2022 respectively.

Overall beef imports to the U.K. were broadly unchanged in the first quarter of 2026. But the latest data from HMRC show beef imports from New Zealand surged to over 12,200 metric tons in the first five months of this year — up around 340 percent from the same period last year, meaning the country had already used almost 60 percent of its quota by May.

Meanwhile, the latest data available for Australia show imports jumped to around 6,500 tons between January and April — an increase of 112 percent.

The figures have reignited concerns among livestock farmers that the trade agreements could eventually lead to a much larger influx of imported meat. Both deals will ultimately grant Australia and New Zealand tariff-free access to the U.K. market for both beef and lamb.

Crossbench peer and beef farmer Minette Batters was among the earliest and most vocal critics of the agreements during her tenure as president of the National Farmers’ Union from 2018 and 2024.

Asked by POLITICO if her concerns of an influx of Aussie and Kiwi meat were materializing, she replied: “Most definitely.”

Batters argued that the trend was likely to intensify as the agreements are fully phased in.

“We paved the way in a decade’s time for completely liberalized relationships,” she said, warning that the U.K. had surrendered many of the safeguards that could have been used to shield domestic producers from a surge in imports.

Current NFU President Tom Bradshaw said the volumes showed a “very worrying trend that risks undermining the confidence of U.K. producers at a time when the whole market is asking for a long-term approach in the face of a very tight global beef inventory.”

Hannah Clarke, a red meat analyst at the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), an industry body for farmers sponsored by the U.K. government, said the increase reflected both the gradual expansion of tariff-free quotas under the trade agreements, as well as wider turbulence in global markets.

As Beijing moves to support domestic production and curb imports, exporters including Australia and New Zealand are increasingly seeking to diversify away from China, helping to redirect trade flows towards markets such as Britain. “China’s effects do ripple,” Clarke said.

Conflict in the Middle East has also disrupted established trade routes, while strong U.K. beef prices have made the British market increasingly attractive to overseas suppliers, she added.

A key concern for cattle farmers was that the Australia deal would lead to an influx of premium cuts such as striploin and rib, putting pressure on British producers in the most lucrative part of the market. This fear, too, appears to be materializing.

“Anecdotally, we understand that Australia are sending higher value products,” said Clarke.

David Barton, chair of the National Farmers’ Union’s livestock board, warned that rising imports were coinciding with falling prices being paid to British cattle farmers, while costs for essentials such as fuel and fertilizer remain high. He urged supermarkets, beef processors and other major buyers to show a “long-term commitment” to sourcing British produce.

Responding to farmers’ concerns, Macaulay Jones, Beef and Lamb New Zealand’s director for the U.K. and EU, pointed out that New Zealand’s share of beef imports had increased “from a very low base, increasing from less than 1 percent of total U.K. beef imports prior to the FTA, to still under 6 percent after three years of improved market access.”

He added that the “seasonal complementarity of production of New Zealand grass-fed red meat and the U.K.’s product allows consumers access to ‘best in season’ product all year round.”

A trade spokesperson for the Australian government said Australian beef and lamb was “regarded as amongst the best quality in the world, underpinning its appeal in the U.K. and around the globe.” They pointed out that, in 2025, U.K. agricultural exports to Australia reached $909 million — the highest on record — which was “largely comparable to the $1.1 billion that Australia exported to the U.K. last year.”

It’s not just the influx of Australian and New Zealand beef that is keeping farmers awake at night. AHDB data show that beef imports from Brazil — a key member of the South American trade bloc known as Mercosur — also rose strongly, increasing 58.7 percent to 8,000 tons in the first quarter of this year.

U.K. Trade Minister Chris Bryant has been vocal in his support for a U.K. free trade agreement with the bloc in the style of the EU’s recent deal, to the fury of British farmers, who fear a similar surge in South American meat.

For some farmers, however, the debate extends beyond import volumes and prices.

Liz Webster, founder of Save British Farming, argued that the issue was “bigger than today’s market movements,” warning that Britain faced growing “geopolitical instability, climate volatility and increasing competition for global food supplies.”

Webster said domestic food production was being squeezed when it should be treated as a “strategic national asset,” and criticized a policy approach that had prioritized “cheap imports and market efficiency” while neglecting resilience.

“The question ministers should be asking,” she added, “is not whether imported beef is marginally cheaper today. It is whether Britain will still have the livestock sector it needs when the next major global shock arrives.”

Batters shares these concerns. In her recent Farming Profitability Review, she argued that stronger country-of-origin labeling was needed to help consumers support British farmers, amid concerns that imported meat is being mislabeled as British.

She called for the voluntary country-of-origin labeling code used by supermarkets to be extended to the out-of-home sector — such as restaurants, pubs, hotels and catering businesses — which accounts for around half of the value of food sales in the U.K.

The system, she said, should be “underpinned by British assurance schemes, so that we don’t see misuse of the Union Jack,” adding that “the consumer is getting massively ripped off here.”

Ironically, Batters noted, Australia and New Zealand both have robust rules designed to help consumers identify and buy genuinely domestic products. “We don’t have anything,” she said, “so the consumer doesn’t know.”

The government is expected to respond to her review later this month.
